1114.title: The table and the tablecloth today
1114.word: The table and the tablecloth today
1114.hook: Karo's code with Isserles' notes, still the reference rabbis reach for
1114.howItsDone: Rabbis and students consult the Shulchan Arukh, printed with the Rema's glosses and later commentaries, when answering questions of daily practice; it is also a core text for those studying toward rabbinic ordination.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tur, and your line: four rows. Prayer, food, family, money. Today, the book that kept those rows and set them out like a table.

A code of law that begins in bed. Its first ruling is about waking up: a person should rise like a lion in the morning to serve the Creator, and be the one who wakes the dawn. Not the dawn waking you. You waking it. That's the opening of a book by Rabbi Joseph Karo. And on the same page, set off from his words, a second rabbi adds a line before Karo's lion even gets out of bed, a verse from the Psalms: "I have set the LORD always before me." Two voices, one page, and the page is still open on desks today.
screen: `RISE LIKE A LION.` → `A SECOND VOICE ON THE PAGE.` → `I HAVE SET THE LORD ALWAYS BEFORE ME.`

segments.voice: You met this pair last year; today, the page as it's used now. First, the table. Karo called his code the Shulchan Arukh, the set table: the law laid out and ready, like a meal with every dish in its place. He had already written a long commentary weighing the earlier authorities, and this was its short, usable form, in brief rulings, following yesterday's four rows. Second, the tablecloth. In Poland, Rabbi Moses Isserles, known as the Rema, saw that in places the set table didn't match the practice of his own Ashkenazi communities, since Karo had leaned on Sephardi authorities. So he didn't write a rival book. He wrote notes, and called them the Mappah, the tablecloth, spread over Karo's table. Third, the page. The two are printed together, Karo's ruling and then, set off, the Rema's gloss. Where they differ, Sephardi communities generally look to Karo and Ashkenazi communities to the Rema: two traditions sharing one table. Fourth, today. The Shulchan Arukh is printed surrounded by commentaries, and a rabbi answering an everyday question about Shabbat, a kosher kitchen or a business dispute may well start there. Over time the table has collected many guests, all arguing politely around the edges. But open it, and it still begins the same way: rise like a lion, and above it, the Rema's line.

1115.title: Mishnah Berurah
1115.hook: the Chafetz Chaim's commentary on daily law
1115.howItsDone: Some who keep Jewish law, especially in Ashkenazi communities, study the Mishnah Berurah a little each day, and teachers use it to answer questions about prayer, blessings, Shabbat and the festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the table and the tablecloth: Karo's code with the Rema's notes, sharing one page. Your line was still the table.

Here is a rabbi known by the name of his book. Rabbi Yisrael Meir Kagan wrote a work on guarding speech: gossip, harmful talk, the small cruelties of conversation. He named it Chafetz Chaim, desiring life, after a verse in the Psalms that asks who desires life and answers, in effect, guard your tongue. The book's name became his name. People still call him the Chafetz Chaim. But he wrote another work too, about the clock of an ordinary day: waking, praying, eating, resting on Shabbat.
screen: `A RABBI CALLED BY HIS BOOK.` → `DESIRING LIFE: GUARD YOUR TONGUE.` → `A SECOND BOOK, ON THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Mishnah Berurah. Turn it four ways. First, what it explains: one row of the set table, Orach Chayim, the path of life. Waking up, blessings, prayer, Shabbat, the festivals. Not money, not marriage. The day. Second, the name. Berurah means clear, clarified. By the Chafetz Chaim's time, generations of commentaries had gathered around the Shulchan Arukh, and they didn't always agree. A person trying simply to know how to keep Shabbat could get lost in the margins. The Mishnah Berurah sets out to make the ruling clear. Third, how it works. It gathers the views of later authorities, weighs them, and then says what to do in practice. Where a matter stays unsettled, it says so, and sometimes notes the more careful path for a person who wants to take it. And it shows its work: a companion section, Sha'ar HaTziyun, lists the sources, and another, Biur Halakhah, carries the longer arguments. Clear on top, reasons underneath. Fourth, where it lives. In Ashkenazi communities that keep the law, it's a familiar book for questions of daily practice, studied a little at a time. And it fits its author. The man who wrote a whole book on guarding speech wrote this one on guarding the hours: the same care for small things, turned from the tongue to the day.
screen: `IT EXPLAINS THE PATH OF LIFE.` · `BERURAH: MADE CLEAR.` · `GATHER, WEIGH, THEN RULE.` · `CARE FOR SMALL THINGS.` · then, large: `CLARIFIED.`

segments.voice: Here's one law from the very start of the path of life: on waking, Jewish law asks a person to wash their hands, pouring water over each hand in turn, before the day begins. Let your hands rest open in your lap now and feel them, the hands that will open doors, hold cups and help someone today.
Mishnah Berurah. Clarified teaching: the Chafetz Chaim's commentary on the laws of the day, gathering the views, weighing them, and making the ruling clear. Today's word.
Your line: clarified. Clear is a kindness to the person trying to follow. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

1116.title: A letter about electricity
1116.hook: rabbis answer questions about electricity, organ donation and fertility treatment
1116.carry: responsa reason from the nearest old case
1116.howItsDone: Jews with a question of practice often ask a rabbi they trust. Rabbis answer in person or in writing, and published responsa from Orthodox, Conservative and Reform authorities are collected and studied.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah Berurah, and your line: clarified. Gather the views, weigh them, make the ruling clear. Today, questions no old book saw coming.

A letter arrives at a rabbi's house with a question no sage in the Talmud ever faced. May an electric light be switched on during Shabbat? Another letter: may a family donate a loved one's organs? Another: what does Jewish law say about a child conceived with a doctor's help? There's no page in the Talmud for electricity, and no paragraph in the codes for a fertility clinic. The rabbi can't simply look it up. So the rabbi does what Jewish teachers have done for a long time: reads, thinks, and writes back.
screen: `A LETTER ARRIVES.` → `NO PAGE FOR ELECTRICITY.` → `THE RABBI WRITES BACK.`

segments.voice: Old law. You met this form last year, rulings sent by letter; today, how it meets what's new. First, the form. The exchange is called she'elot u-teshuvot, questions and answers; in English, responsa. A person or a community writes with a real problem, and a rabbi answers in writing, with reasons. Collections of these letters line the shelves of Jewish libraries. Second, the method. No verse mentions electricity, so the rabbi looks for the nearest case the old law did discuss. The Torah forbids kindling fire throughout your dwellings on the Sabbath day. Is a glowing bulb a kind of fire? Is closing a circuit a kind of building, finishing something so that it works? Or is it something else entirely? Each answer depends on which old case the new one is most like. Third, the disagreement. Because the comparison decides so much, careful rabbis reading the same sources can reach different answers. On organ donation, much turns on how the moment of death is understood, and authorities answer differently. Orthodox rabbis, Conservative law committees and Reform rabbinic bodies all write responsa, each in their own way. Fourth, the person. A responsum answers someone: a family at a hospital bed, a couple who want a child. The law isn't consulted from a distance; it's asked, by name, in the middle of a life. That's why the old law keeps speaking: people keep bringing it questions, and someone keeps writing back.
screen: `QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS, BY LETTER.` · `IS A BULB LIKE FIRE?` · `SAME SOURCES, DIFFERENT ANSWERS.` · `A REAL PERSON IS ASKING.` · then, large: `REASON FROM THE NEAREST OLD CASE.`

1117.title: Dig under the wall
1117.hook: the principle of saving life shapes modern debates; answers differ by community
1117.carry: live by them, not die by them
1117.howItsDone: Jews who keep Shabbat and the fasts set them aside when a life may be in danger, calling for help, driving to a hospital or eating on Yom Kippur when doctors say so. Families facing medical decisions often consult a rabbi alongside their doctors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a letter arrived, and your line: responsa reason from the nearest old case. Today, the rule that comes before almost every other.

Shabbat afternoon. A wall comes down, and stones cover a corner of the courtyard. Is someone under there? Nobody's sure. If someone is, are they alive? Nobody knows. On a day when work stops, when even moving stones is restricted, what happens next? The Mishnah does not hesitate. Clear the stones. Even if it's doubtful anyone is there. Even if it's doubtful they're alive. Even if nobody knows whether the person under them is Jewish or not. Dig.
screen: `A WALL FALLS ON SHABBAT.` → `IS SOMEONE UNDER THERE?` → `DIG.`

segments.voice: Saving life first. In Hebrew, pikuach nefesh. You met it in year two; today, how far it reaches. First, doubt is enough. The Mishnah in tractate Yoma says that wherever there is a doubt of danger to life, it sets Shabbat aside. You don't need certainty before you act. Second, the source. The Talmud asks where this comes from, and offers several answers. One it lands on is a verse in Leviticus about God's laws: "which if a man do, he shall live by them." Live by them, the Talmud says, and not die by them. The commandments are meant for living. Third, the limits. Saving life sets aside almost everything, but not quite everything. The Talmud names a few things a person may not do even to save their own life, among them taking another person's life. One life is not bought with another. Fourth, today. This principle sits in the middle of hard modern questions. When must a sick person eat on Yom Kippur? The Mishnah already says a sick person is fed when experts say so. How hard should doctors push at the end of a life? Here, honestly, answers differ, between communities and within them. What they share is the starting point: life comes first, and the arguments are about what that requires. A rule built for living.
screen: `DOUBT IS ENOUGH.` · `HE SHALL LIVE BY THEM.` · `THE LIMITS: NOT ANOTHER'S LIFE.` · `TODAY'S HARD QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `LIVE BY THEM, NOT DIE BY THEM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who might sit beside you if you were ever very sick, and see their face. Ask yourself, quietly and without hurry, what you'd want them to know about treatment, comfort, and who should decide if you can't; you don't need answers now. If any of this weighs on you, or you're in danger yourself, you don't have to hold it alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach your local emergency help.
Saving life first. Pikuach nefesh: the principle that saving a life sets aside nearly every commandment, even Shabbat. Today's word.
Your line: live by them, not die by them. The commandments are meant for living. Take care of yourself, and see you tomorrow.

1118.title: Still arguing, for heaven's sake
1118.hook: Jews still argue over law, for heaven's sake
1118.carry: an argument for heaven's sake endures
1118.howItsDone: Jewish learning is often done aloud with a study partner, a chavruta, whose job is to question and push back. Rabbis and movements publish differing rulings and debate them openly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saving life first: a wall falls on Shabbat, and you dig, even in doubt. Live by the commandments, not die by them. Today, an argument with real stakes.

Two schools of sages, the house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, disagreed about marriage law. Not about table manners: about which marriages were valid at all, which is about as high as the stakes get. Each side, by its own reasoning, could look at some of the other's marriages and see a problem. And the Mishnah reports what happened next. They married into each other's families anyway. They kept arguing, and the families kept joining. Today's word is how a tradition manages that.
screen: `HILLEL'S HOUSE, SHAMMAI'S HOUSE.` → `A FIGHT OVER MARRIAGE LAW.` → `THEY MARRIED EACH OTHER ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Still arguing. You met the Mishnah's test last year; today, what it asks of an argument. First, the test. Pirkei Avot says that every argument for the sake of heaven will in the end endure, and every argument not for the sake of heaven will not endure. In Hebrew, machloket l'shem shamayim: an argument about what is true and right, not about winning. Second, the examples. Which argument was for the sake of heaven? The argument of Hillel and Shammai. Which was not? The argument of Korah and all his company, the rebellion against Moses in the wilderness. Some readers notice an odd detail: for Hillel and Shammai, both sides are named. For Korah, Moses isn't named as a side at all. One reading: Korah's company was never really arguing with Moses. Each of them was arguing for himself. Third, the wedding. That's what makes the report about marriage so striking. The two houses disagreed where it mattered most, and still did not stop marrying into each other's families. The argument and the relationship both survived. Fourth, today. Jews are still arguing over law. Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist Jews read the tradition differently, and inside each, rabbis disagree again, as the last two days showed. In a study hall, a learning partner is supposed to push back; a quiet room might mean nobody's thinking. The Mishnah's question still sits on every argument: is this for heaven's sake, or for mine?

1119.title: Finishing a tractate
1119.hook: a celebration when a tractate is completed
1119.howItsDone: When a person or group completes a tractate, they hold a siyum: the last passage is read, the hadran is recited, someone teaches a few words on the tractate, and a festive meal follows. A siyum is often held on the morning before Passover so that firstborns may join the meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, still arguing: Hillel's and Shammai's houses kept disagreeing and kept marrying each other. Today, what happens when a book is finished.

The last line of a tractate. Someone reads it aloud, slowly, and the room that has been quiet for an hour suddenly isn't. A cake appears from somewhere. Someone pours a drink. Someone else stands up to say a few words about the final page, gets interrupted, and starts again. Months of study, sometimes years, one page at a time, and now the book is closed. It is not a quiet moment. It's a party. Today's word is the name of that party.
screen: `THE LAST LINE, READ ALOUD.` → `A CAKE APPEARS.` → `A BOOK CLOSES. A PARTY STARTS.`

segments.voice: Siyum. Completion, and the celebration that marks it. First, an old feast. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, tells of the sage Abaye saying that whenever he saw a young scholar finish a tractate, he made a feast for the rabbis. Notice whose finish it was. Not his own. He threw the party for somebody else's last page. Second, what's said. At a siyum, those who finished say a short traditional text called the hadran. It speaks to the tractate itself, by name, as if to a friend: we will return to you, and you will return to us. We won't forget you, and you won't forget us. The ending isn't goodbye; it's see you again. Third, the meal. The meal after a siyum is treated as a seudat mitzvah, a meal that is itself part of a commandment, like the meal at a wedding or a circumcision. A custom grows out of that. On the day before Passover, by custom, firstborns fast. Some attend a siyum that morning, and joining its meal releases them from the fast. Fourth, the size. A siyum can be three people around a kitchen table who finished a small tractate together, or a crowd in a large hall when a daily study cycle reaches the end of the whole Talmud. Same words, same promise to return.

1120.title: Beruriah and the open page
1120.hook: women study Talmud today; communities differ about how
1120.carry: beruriah read closely, and the page kept her
1120.howItsDone: Women study Talmud in women's study halls, synagogue classes, university courses and daily page cycles, alone or with a study partner. Communities differ in what they offer and encourage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the siyum: finish the page, then promise to return. This week laid the table and its cloth, made the law clear, met new questions, put life first, kept arguing, and finished a book. Today, who gets to open it.

Some rough neighbors were making Rabbi Meir's life miserable, the Talmud says, so miserable that he prayed they would die. His wife, Beruriah, stopped him. What are you basing this on? He pointed to a verse in the Psalms: let sinners cease out of the earth. Read it again, she said. The Hebrew can be read as sins, not sinners. Let sins cease. And look at the end of the verse: then the wicked will be no more. Pray that they turn back, and there will be no more wicked. He did, and the Talmud says they turned back. A woman, reading closely, correcting a sage.

segments.voice: The page is open. You met Beruriah and Ben Azzai last year; today, where that old argument stands now. First, Beruriah. She appears in the Talmud by name, as a sharp reader of scripture, and her argument turns on a single word. The sages kept her reading on the page. Second, an old disagreement, kept honestly. The Mishnah in tractate Sotah records two views. Ben Azzai says a man is obligated to teach his daughter Torah. Rabbi Eliezer objects, and says teaching a daughter Torah is like teaching her foolishness. Both views stay in the Mishnah, side by side, and later generations had to decide which one to walk by. Third, today. Women study Talmud in classes, in study halls, with study partners and in daily page-a-day cycles, and some have celebrated finishing the whole of it. Communities differ on this, and say so openly. Orthodox communities disagree among themselves about how and what women should study, with some building serious programs of Talmud study for women and others holding back. Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist movements teach Talmud to women and men alike, including in rabbinic training. Fourth, the page itself. In Hebrew, a page of Talmud is a daf. Remember the Vilna edition: the same page everywhere. The page doesn't check who opened it. It just asks to be read closely, the way Beruriah read.
